questions.q: Which of these shows the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism in the correct order, from smallest to largest?
o: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Cell, organ, tissue, organ system, organism
Tissue, cell, organ, organ system, organism
Cell, tissue, organ system, organ, organism
questions.a: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism: similar cells form a tissue, more than one type of tissue forms an organ, organs form organ systems and organ systems form the organism.

questions.q: Which statement about an amoeba is correct?
o: Its single cell performs all the functions of life
Different tissues in its body share the work of living
It uses muscle tissue to move and nervous tissue to carry messages
Its organs are grouped into organ systems
questions.a: Its single cell performs all the functions of life; an amoeba is unicellular, so it has no tissues or organs.

questions.q:
Match each job (Column I) with the tissue that does it (Column II).
Column I: 1. Movement in animals  2. Carrying messages to different parts of an animal's body  3. Carrying water and minerals in a plant  4. Carrying food in a plant
Column II: (a) Phloem  (b) Muscle tissue  (c) Xylem  (d) Nervous tissue
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-c, 4-a: muscle tissue enables movement, nervous tissue carries messages, xylem transports water and minerals, and phloem transports food.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Forming different types of tissues increases the efficiency of a multicellular body.
Reason (R): In multicellular organisms, different groups of cells perform different functions, which is a division of labour.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: different tissues lead to a division of labour, and the division of labour is what increases the body's efficiency.

questions.q: Define a tissue and give one example of a tissue found in animals.
questions.a: A tissue is a group of cells, similar in structure, that work together to perform a specific function. Example: muscle tissue (which enables movement) or nervous tissue (which carries messages).
s: Definition: a group of similar cells working together for a specific function
One correct animal tissue, such as muscle tissue or nervous tissue

questions.q: True or False: Plants and animals have different tissues only because animals move and plants do not; they get their food in the same way. Give the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Movement is one reason, but their mode of nutrition also differs: animals have tissues to digest food obtained from outside sources, while plants have tissues that use solar energy to make food by photosynthesis.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: nutrition also differs; animals digest food from outside, plants make food by photosynthesis using solar energy

questions.q:
(a) Why do most plants need support?
(b) What part of a plant cell gives it rigidity and strength?
(c) How does the absence of a rigid cell wall help animals?
questions.a: (a) Most plants are fixed in one place and must stay firm and upright. (b) The cell wall. (c) Without a rigid wall, animal cells can change shape easily, and this flexibility makes their bodies suitable for locomotion.
s: (a) Plants are fixed in one place and need to stay firm and upright
(b) The cell wall gives rigidity and strength
(c) Animal cells can change shape easily, which suits the body for locomotion

questions.q: Meena says, 'A leaf is a tissue, because every cell in it is a plant cell.' Judge her claim using the meaning of a tissue and of an organ.
questions.a: She is wrong. A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one specific function; being plant cells is not enough. A leaf has more than one type of tissue (for example the epidermis with stomata, and the xylem and phloem of its veins), and more than one type of tissue together forms an organ. So a leaf is an organ, not a tissue.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
A tissue is a group of similar cells for one function, not just any group of plant cells
A leaf has several tissue types (e.g. epidermis, xylem, phloem), so it is an organ

questions.q:
A student examines one structure taken from an animal and records:
Record 1: it is made of a very large number of cells.
Record 2: one part is a group of similar muscle cells that contract together.
Record 3: its inner lining is a layer of cells specialised to produce and release mucus and enzymes.
Record 4: it works together with several other such structures to carry out one life process.
(a) Which two records show that the structure is not a single tissue? Explain.
(b) Using your answer to (a), name the level of organisation of the structure.
(c) Which record places it inside a higher level, and what is that level called?
(d) A classmate says the structure could be part of an amoeba. Use Record 1 and the levels of organisation to reject this.
questions.a: (a) Records 2 and 3: they describe two different types of tissue (muscle tissue, and an epithelium specialised for secretion). A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one specific function, so a structure with two tissue types is not a single tissue. (b) More than one type of tissue together forms an organ, so the structure is an organ. (c) Record 4: different organs working together form an organ system. (d) An amoeba is unicellular: its single cell performs all the functions of life, so it has no tissues or organs. The structure has many cells and two tissue types, so it must come from a multicellular organism.
s: (a) Records 2 and 3 show two different tissue types, so it is not one tissue
(b) More than one tissue type forms an organ: it is an organ
(c) Record 4: organs working together form an organ system
(d) Amoeba is one cell doing all functions, with no tissues or organs, so the claim is rejected

questions.q:
A blade of grass and a pet dog are compared.
(a) Which of the two has cells with a rigid cell wall?
(b) Why does that organism need such a wall?
(c) Which of the two has cells that can change shape easily, and how does this help it?
(d) Which of the two has tissues that digest food obtained from outside sources?
(e) How does the other organism get its food?
questions.a: (a) The grass. (b) It is fixed in one place and needs support to stay firm and upright. (c) The dog; its cells lack a rigid wall and change shape easily, which suits its body for locomotion. (d) The dog. (e) The grass makes its own food by photosynthesis, using solar energy.
s: (a) The grass
(b) It is fixed in one place and needs support to stay upright
(c) The dog; flexible cells suit its body for movement
(d) The dog
(e) The grass makes food by photosynthesis using solar energy

questions.q: Which tissue makes the stem of a plant grow in girth (thickness)?
questions.a: Lateral meristem, a ring of actively dividing cells in the stem that adds new cells inside and outside.

questions.q: Grass in a field grows back a few days after cows graze on it. Which tissue makes this regrowth possible?
o: Intercalary meristem at the nodes of the stem
Apical meristem at the root tips
Lateral meristem arranged in a ring in the stem
questions.a: Intercalary meristem at the nodes of the stem, which helps plants such as grasses regenerate after cutting or grazing.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of meristematic cells?
o: A large, prominent nucleus and dense cytoplasm
A large vacuole and loose packing with big spaces
Cells that are dead when mature
questions.a: A large, prominent nucleus and dense cytoplasm; meristematic cells are also small, thin-walled, usually without vacuoles and tightly packed.

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement I: The part of a stem between two nodes is called the internode.
Statement II: Intercalary meristem is found at the tip of the root.
Statement III: Cells that lose the ability to divide become permanent tissue through differentiation.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Only I and III. Statement II is wrong: intercalary meristem lies at the base of the internode or just above the node; the root tip has apical meristem.

questions.q:
(a) Name the meristem found at the tips of roots and shoots.
(b) What kind of growth does it bring about?
questions.a: (a) Apical meristem. (b) Growth in length: height of the stem and depth of the roots.
s: (a) Apical meristem
(b) Growth in length of root and shoot

questions.q: True or False: Meristematic cells have large vacuoles, and this is what lets them divide rapidly. Give the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Vacuoles are generally absent in meristematic cells. Their small size, thin walls, large nucleus, dense cytoplasm and tight packing are what allow continuous and rapid division.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: vacuoles are generally absent; dense cytoplasm, large nucleus, thin walls allow rapid division

questions.q: State the three ways in which plants grow, and name the meristem responsible for each.
questions.a: Increase in length (height of stem and depth of roots): apical meristem. Increase in girth (thickness of stem): lateral meristem. Regrowth after cutting or grazing: intercalary meristem.
s: Growth in length: apical meristem
Growth in girth: lateral meristem
Regrowth after cutting or grazing: intercalary meristem

questions.q: A student labels a slide 'Meristematic tissue from a shoot tip' and notes: cells loosely packed with large spaces between them, each with a big vacuole. Show that the label cannot be correct.
questions.a: Meristematic cells are tightly packed with little or no intercellular space, so loose packing does not fit. Vacuoles are generally absent in meristematic cells, so big vacuoles do not fit either. These features (loosely packed, with spaces) match a permanent tissue such as parenchyma, not a dividing tissue; meristem needs its dense, tightly packed cells for continuous rapid division.
s: Meristem is tightly packed with little or no intercellular space
Meristematic cells generally lack vacuoles
The described cells match a permanent tissue like parenchyma, not a rapidly dividing one

questions.q:
A student studies a slide of meristematic tissue from an onion root tip. Answer from what the slide shows.
(a) Are the cell walls thin or thick?
(b) Is the nucleus small or large and prominent?
(c) Are vacuoles generally present or absent?
(d) Are the cells tightly packed or loosely arranged with large gaps between them?
questions.a: (a) Thin cell walls. (b) A large and prominent nucleus. (c) Vacuoles are generally absent. (d) Tightly packed, with little or no intercellular space. These features suit continuous and rapid cell division.
s: (a) Thin cell walls
(b) Large, prominent nucleus
(c) Vacuoles generally absent
(d) Tightly packed, little or no intercellular space

questions.q:
A section of a root shows two zones. Zone X, right at the tip: small cells with thin walls, a large nucleus, dense cytoplasm, no vacuoles, tightly packed. Zone Y, a little further up: larger cells, some joined into tubes that carry water.
(a) Identify the tissue in zone X and give two features from the description that support it.
(b) How did the cells of zone Y come from cells like those in zone X? Name the process.
(c) Predict what would happen to the length of the root if zone X were destroyed, and give the reason.
(d) Explain how the features of zone X suit its job.
questions.a: (a) Apical meristem; supported by any two of: thin walls, large prominent nucleus, dense cytoplasm, no vacuoles, tight packing. (b) The new cells lost the ability to divide and changed in structure and function to become specialised permanent tissue; this is differentiation. (c) The root would stop growing in length, because roots grow only from their tips, where the dividing cells are. (d) These features allow continuous and rapid cell division, which keeps adding new cells to the root.
s: (a) Apical meristem identified
(a) Two supporting features from the description
(b) Differentiation: cells stop dividing and become specialised permanent tissue
(c) Root stops lengthening because roots grow only from their tips
(d) The features allow continuous, rapid division

questions.q: What is the main job of the waxy cuticle that covers the epidermis of a plant?
o: Making the stem grow in girth
questions.a: Reducing water loss: the cuticle is a waxy layer of cutin that cuts down water loss and also protects against mechanical injury and parasites.

questions.q: Which cells of the phloem carry food from the leaves to other parts of the plant?
questions.a: Sieve tubes, long tubular cells joined end to end by perforated walls.

questions.q:
Match each plant tissue (Column I) with its feature (Column II).
Column I: 1. Parenchyma  2. Collenchyma  3. Sclerenchyma  4. Epidermis
Column II: (a) Thick walls with lignin; most cells dead  (b) A single layer of tightly packed flat cells  (c) Living cells with thin walls, loosely packed  (d) Living cells with corners thickened by pectin
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: parenchyma is living and thin-walled, collenchyma has pectin-thickened corners, sclerenchyma has lignified walls and is mostly dead, and the epidermis is a single tightly packed layer.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Xylem is a complex permanent tissue.
Reason (R): Xylem is made of only one type of cell, the tracheid.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: xylem is complex because it is made of different types of cells (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres) working together.

questions.q: Give two functions of the stomata found in the epidermis of leaves.
questions.a: Stomata allow gaseous exchange, and they help in transpiration (evaporation of water vapour), which helps water transport and removal of wastes.
s: Gaseous exchange
Transpiration (evaporation of water vapour through the pores)

questions.q: True or False: If the companion cells beside a sieve tube are damaged, the loading and unloading of sugars in that sieve tube will be disturbed, even though the sieve tube itself is unharmed. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The sieve tube carries the food, but its cellular functions are regulated by the companion cells, whose main job is to monitor the loading and unloading of sugars in the sieve tube. If the companion cells are damaged, this monitoring stops, so sugar loading and unloading is disturbed.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: companion cells regulate the sieve tube cells and monitor sugar loading and unloading, so damage to them disturbs it

questions.q:
(a) Name the three simple permanent tissues.
(b) Which of them mainly stores food?
(c) Which of them forms hard coverings such as a walnut shell?
questions.a: (a) Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. (b) Parenchyma. (c) Sclerenchyma.
s: (a) Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma
(b) Parenchyma
(c) Sclerenchyma

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Phloem is just like xylem: it is mostly dead cells, and it carries water up from the roots.' Check each part of his claim.
questions.a: Both parts are wrong. Phloem is mostly made of living cells (unlike xylem, whose tracheids, vessels and fibres are mainly sclerenchymatous). Phloem's sieve tubes carry food from the leaves to other parts of the plant; it is xylem that carries water and minerals from the roots.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong in both parts
Phloem is mostly living cells, unlike xylem
Phloem carries food from leaves; xylem carries water and minerals from roots

questions.q:
A school botany club in Shillong studies one sector of a stem section under a microscope. They record: an outer single layer of tightly packed flat cells with a waxy coat; 40 thin-walled living cells with spaces between them, some green; 15 living cells with thickened corners; 25 cells with very thick walls and no living contents; thick-walled tubes that carry water and minerals up the stem; and tubes joined end to end by perforated walls, with small cells beside them.
(a) Name the tissue of the 40 cells and give one job it does.
(b) Of the 80 cells counted in the ground tissue, what percentage are dead?
(c) Name the perforated tubes and the small cells beside them.
(d) The club says this section shows all three tissue systems. Do you agree? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Parenchyma; it mainly stores food (and its green cells photosynthesise). (b) The 25 thick-walled cells (sclerenchyma) are dead: 25/80 x 100 = 31.25%, about 31%. (c) Sieve tubes and companion cells (phloem). (d) Yes: the outer layer is the dermal system (epidermis with cuticle), the parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma form the ground system, and the water-carrying tubes (xylem) with the sieve tubes (phloem) form the vascular system.
s: (a) Parenchyma, with one job (storing food or photosynthesis)
(c) Sieve tubes and companion cells
(d) Yes: dermal (epidermis), ground (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma), vascular (xylem and phloem)

questions.q:
Ravi's revision table on plant tissues reads:
Row 1: Parenchyma - dead cells with thick walls - stores food.
Row 2: Collenchyma - living cells, corners thickened by pectin - lets stems and tendrils bend without breaking.
Row 3: Sclerenchyma - living cells with thin walls - found in coconut husk.
Row 4: Xylem - tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres - carries food from leaves.
Row 5: Phloem - sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres - carries food from leaves.
Judge each row as correct or wrong, and correct every error.
questions.a: Row 1 is wrong: parenchyma has living cells with thin walls (it does store food). Row 2 is correct. Row 3 is wrong: sclerenchyma has thick walls due to lignin and most cells are dead (coconut husk is correct). Row 4 is wrong: xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to other parts (its cell list is correct). Row 5 is correct.
s: Row 1 wrong: parenchyma is living and thin-walled
Row 2 correct
Row 3 wrong: sclerenchyma has thick lignified walls, mostly dead
Row 4 wrong: xylem carries water and minerals from roots
Row 5 correct

questions.q: Which epithelium is found in the skin, mouth and oesophagus?
o: Many layers of cells, with the outer cells flat and tightly packed
A single layer of thin, flat cells
A single layer of tall, pillar-like cells
questions.a: Many layers of cells, with the outer cells flat and tightly packed; this protective epithelium guards underlying tissues from injury, friction and microbes.

questions.q: Blood and bone are both connective tissues, yet blood is fluid and bone is hard. What causes this difference?
o: Their matrix: watery and jelly-like in blood, hard and rigid in bone
Bone cells have cell walls but blood cells do not
Blood cells have many nuclei but bone cells have none
Bone is a muscular tissue while blood is a connective tissue
questions.a: Their matrix: it is watery, soft and jelly-like in blood but hard, solid and rigid in bone.

questions.q: A blood test shows that a person has far fewer platelets than normal. Which problem is this person most likely to face?
o: A small cut takes much longer to stop bleeding
The skin turns red during exercise
The bones become soft and bend easily
questions.a: A small cut takes much longer to stop bleeding, because platelets help blood clot at the site of injury.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ligaments help prevent dislocation of a joint.
Reason (R): Tendons connect muscles to bones.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: ligaments prevent dislocation because they connect bone to bone and limit movement; what tendons do does not explain this.

questions.q:
(a) What percentage of the total volume of blood is plasma?
(b) What percentage is made up of the formed elements (blood cells and platelets)?
questions.a: (a) Plasma is about 55% of the total volume. (b) The formed elements are about 45%.
s: (a) Plasma: 55%
(b) Formed elements: 45%

questions.q: True or False: Your outer ear springs back to its shape after you fold it, so it must be made of bone, like the hard part you feel at your elbow. Give the reason.
questions.a: False. Keeping its shape does not make it bone. The ear can be folded and then retains its shape, which is cartilage: a soft, flexible tissue with a jelly-like matrix. Bone has a rigid matrix of calcium and phosphorus compounds, so it is hard and could not be folded at all.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the ear folds and regains shape, so it is cartilage (soft, jelly-like matrix); bone is rigid and cannot fold

questions.q:
For each function of epithelial tissue, give one place in the body where it is found:
(a) secretion
(b) sensory functions such as smell and taste
(c) rapid exchange of gases
questions.a: (a) Salivary glands, sweat glands or the stomach lining. (b) Nostrils, taste buds or the inner ear. (c) The lining of the lungs or of blood vessels.
s: (a) Salivary glands, sweat glands or stomach lining
(b) Nostrils, taste buds or inner ear
(c) Lining of lungs or blood vessels

questions.q:
Suppose an illness changes the lining of a child's small intestine: its tall, pillar-like cells become thin and flat, and their hair-like structures are lost.
(a) Which function of epithelial tissue does the healthy lining perform?
(b) Describe the healthy structure that suits this function.
(c) Predict how the change would affect the child, and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Absorption: efficient uptake of nutrients and water. (b) A single layer of tall, pillar-like cells, often with hair-like structures. (c) The child would take up nutrients and water less efficiently, because epithelial tissues are structurally adapted to their function; thin flat cells suit rapid exchange by diffusion (as in blood vessels and lungs), not efficient uptake.
s: (a) Absorption: efficient uptake of nutrients and water
(b) Single layer of tall, pillar-like cells, often with hair-like structures
(c) Less efficient uptake of nutrients and water, since structure is adapted to function

questions.q:
A pathology lab in Lucknow lets a 10 mL blood sample settle in a tube. It separates into two layers: an upper liquid layer and a lower layer containing the cells and platelets. The technician notes that the proportions match those of normal blood.
(a) Name the upper liquid layer and find its volume.
(b) Name the lower layer and find its volume.
(c) Which cell in the lower layer gives blood its red colour?
(d) Which part of the lower layer would help a cut to clot?
questions.a: (a) Plasma: 55% of 10 mL = 5.5 mL. (b) Formed elements: 45% of 10 mL = 4.5 mL. (c) Red blood cells (RBCs), because of haemoglobin. (d) Platelets.
s: (a) Plasma, 5.5 mL
(b) Formed elements, 4.5 mL
(c) Red blood cells
(d) Platelets

questions.q:
Students build a model of a knee. They use: two hard plastic rods for the leg bones; rubber pads on the rod ends where they meet; elastic bands joining one rod to the other; and strings joining a balloon 'muscle' to one rod.
(a)-(d) Name the connective tissue each of the four model parts stands for, with the function that makes it a good copy.
(e) One group replaces the elastic bands with stiff steel wire. Evaluate this change.
questions.a: (a) Plastic rods: bone, hard and rigid, giving strength and support. (b) Rubber pads: cartilage, which cushions the ends of bones for shock absorption. (c) Elastic bands joining rod to rod: ligaments, which connect bone to bone, give stability and limit movement. (d) Strings from balloon to rod: tendons, which connect muscle to bone and bring about movement. (e) A poor change: ligaments limit movement but still allow the joint to bend; stiff wire would lock the rods so the knee model could not move at all.
s: (a) Rods = bone (strength, support)
(b) Rubber pads = cartilage (cushioning, shock absorption)
(c) Elastic bands = ligaments (bone to bone, limit movement)
(d) Strings = tendons (muscle to bone, movement)
(e) Steel wire is a poor copy: it would stop the joint moving, while ligaments only limit movement

questions.q: Which type of muscle is found in the walls of the stomach and intestines?
questions.a: Smooth muscle, which brings about slow, continuous movements such as those of digestion.

questions.q: Which part of a neuron receives signals from other neurons?
questions.a: Dendrites receive signals from other neurons.

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement I: Skeletal muscles are attached to the skeleton and carry out voluntary movements.
Statement II: Smooth muscle cells have a single nucleus and lack striations.
Statement III: Cardiac muscle fibres are cylindrical and branched, with a single nucleus.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III. All three are correct: skeletal muscle is attached to the skeleton and does voluntary movements, smooth muscle cells have one nucleus and no striations, and cardiac fibres are cylindrical, branched and have a single nucleus.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Writing with a pen is a voluntary movement.
Reason (R): Writing is carried out by smooth muscles, which bring about slow, continuous movements.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: writing is under conscious control and is carried out by skeletal muscles; smooth muscles bring about involuntary movements such as digestion.

questions.q:
(a) Where in the body are cardiac muscles found?
(b) Why can the heart beat throughout life without getting tired?
questions.a: (a) Only in the heart. (b) Cardiac muscles work tirelessly and rhythmically, so the heart beats throughout life without fatigue.
s: (a) Only in the heart
(b) Cardiac muscle works tirelessly and rhythmically, without fatigue

questions.q: True or False: In a neuron, the axon receives messages from other neurons and carries them towards the cell body. Give the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Dendrites receive signals from other neurons; the axon is a long fibre that carries messages away from the cell and ends at axon terminals, which pass the messages to other cells.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: dendrites receive signals; the axon carries messages from the cell to the axon terminals

questions.q:
Say whether each movement is voluntary or involuntary, and name the type of muscle that does it.
(a) Lifting a school bag
(b) Food moving through the intestine
(c) The beating of the heart
questions.a: (a) Voluntary; skeletal muscle. (b) Involuntary; smooth muscle. (c) Involuntary; cardiac muscle.
s: (a) Voluntary, skeletal muscle
(b) Involuntary, smooth muscle
(c) Involuntary, cardiac muscle

questions.q: A slide label reads: 'Muscle from the stomach wall: long, cylindrical, unbranched fibres with many nuclei and light and dark bands.' Show that this label cannot be correct.
questions.a: The stomach wall has smooth muscle, whose cells are spindle-shaped, have a single nucleus and lack striations. The label describes fibres that are cylindrical, multinucleate and striated, which are the features of skeletal muscle, the muscle attached to the skeleton. So the description and the source on the label cannot both be right.
s: Stomach wall has smooth muscle
Smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, single nucleus, no striations
The described features are those of skeletal muscle, so the label is wrong

questions.q: Rina hears the lunch bell, remembers that her tiffin is in her bag, walks to the canteen and eats. Later the food moves along her intestine. Explain, step by step, which tissues are at work and how they are linked.
questions.a: Nervous tissue senses the bell and the brain, the control centre, coordinates the response and her memory of the tiffin. Walking is a voluntary movement done by skeletal muscles attached to the skeleton (long, unbranched, multinucleate, striated fibres). Moving food along the intestine is involuntary, done by smooth muscle (spindle-shaped, single nucleus, no striations) in slow, continuous movements. Neither muscle works on its own: both receive instructions from nervous tissue.
s: Nervous tissue senses; the brain coordinates and remembers
Walking: voluntary, by skeletal muscle
Food movement: involuntary, by smooth muscle
Both muscles act on instructions from nervous tissue

questions.q:
A physiology lab records how the muscle in three organs behaves.
Organ A: contracts rhythmically about 70 times a minute, day and night, and never needs a rest.
Organ B: contracts only when the person decides to lift a weight.
Organ C: contracts slowly and continuously for hours, pushing food along.
The lab also has three unlabelled slides, one from each organ.
Slide 1: long, cylindrical, unbranched fibres with many nuclei and clear light and dark bands.
Slide 2: spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus and no bands.
Slide 3: cylindrical, branched fibres with one nucleus and faint bands.
(a) From its behaviour, name the muscle type in each organ.
(b) Match each slide to its organ, giving the feature that settles each match.
(c) For a sports project the lab head wants the slide of the muscle under conscious control. Which slide should she pick? Apart from the light and dark bands, which ONE feature seen on the slides is enough on its own to rule out the other two?
questions.a: (a) Organ A works rhythmically without fatigue, so it is cardiac muscle (the heart). Organ B moves only by choice, so it is skeletal (voluntary) muscle. Organ C makes slow, continuous movement of food, so it is smooth muscle. (b) Slide 3 (branched, one nucleus, faint bands) is cardiac, so it is from Organ A. Slide 1 (unbranched, many nuclei, clear bands) is skeletal, so it is from Organ B. Slide 2 (spindle-shaped, no bands) is smooth, so it is from Organ C. (c) Slide 1, from Organ B. Apart from the bands, having many nuclei settles it: skeletal fibres are multinucleate, while both smooth and cardiac cells have a single nucleus.
s: (a) A = cardiac, B = skeletal, C = smooth, each with its behaviour as the reason
(b) Slide 3 to A (branched, faint bands), Slide 1 to B (unbranched, many nuclei), Slide 2 to C (spindle-shaped, no bands)
(c) Slide 1; many nuclei (apart from the bands) alone rules out the other two, which have a single nucleus

questions.q: What type of joint is found at the shoulder?
questions.a: Ball and socket joint: the rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone.

questions.q: At the back the ribs are attached to the spine. To which bone are they attached at the front?
questions.a: The breast bone (sternum); the ribs are joined to it by flexible cartilage.

questions.q:
Match each structure (Column I) with its job (Column II).
Column I: 1. Cartilage disc between vertebrae  2. Rib cage  3. Kneecap  4. Skull
Column II: (a) Protects the knee joint  (b) A hard case that protects the brain, eyes and ears  (c) Cushions and lets us bend and twist  (d) Protects the heart and lungs
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: the disc cushions and gives flexibility, the rib cage protects the heart and lungs, the kneecap protects the knee joint, and the skull protects the brain, eyes and ears.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The knee bends and straightens in one direction only.
Reason (R): A small bone called the kneecap protects the knee joint.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the knee moves in one direction because it is a hinge joint, like the elbow; the kneecap only protects that joint, it does not decide how the knee moves.

questions.q:
(a) What is a joint?
(b) Name the type of joint that connects the skull to the backbone.
questions.a: (a) A joint is a junction between two or more bones. (b) A pivot joint.
s: (a) A junction between two or more bones
(b) Pivot joint

questions.q: True or False: Anu decides to lift her school bag, yet her arm muscles cannot do it by themselves; the musculoskeletal system needs another body system to make the lift happen. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The musculoskeletal system works under the control of the nervous system. Muscles, even voluntary ones, cannot function independently; they receive instructions from the nervous tissue, and only then contract and pull on the bones through tendons.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the system works under the control of the nervous system; muscles need instructions from nervous tissue

questions.q:
(a) Name any four parts that make up the musculoskeletal system.
(b) State two things this system helps us do.
(c) Which system controls the musculoskeletal system?
questions.a: (a) Any four of: bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons, ligaments. (b) Any two of: stand upright, move, maintain posture, protect delicate organs. (c) The nervous system.
s: (a) Any four of bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons, ligaments
(b) Any two of: stand upright, move, keep posture, protect delicate organs
(c) The nervous system

questions.q:
(a) Give one everyday action that uses the pivot joint between the skull and the backbone.
(b) What type of joint joins the bones of the skull to each other, and how much movement does it allow?
(c) Explain why it helps the body that the neck joint and the skull joints are of different types.
questions.a: (a) Turning the head from side to side, for example to follow a bird flying past a window. (b) Fixed joints: the skull bones cannot move at all. (c) The pivot joint lets the head turn to look around, while the fixed joints keep the skull a hard, unmoving case, so the brain stays safe even when the body and head move.
s: (a) A correct side-to-side head action (e.g. turning to follow a bird)
(b) Fixed joints; the skull bones cannot move
(c) Pivot lets the head turn; fixed joints keep the skull rigid so the brain stays safe while moving

questions.q:
A robotics club in Pune is building a robot that copies the human body. Their plan for the joints reads: shoulder - a hinge; neck (head to backbone) - a pivot; elbow - a hinge; the plates of the robot's head case - joined by hinges so they can fold. They add that motors placed inside the joints will move the parts, 'just as our joints move our bones'.
(a) Which two choices copy the human body correctly?
(b) What could the robot's arm not do with a hinge at the shoulder?
(c) Why should the head-case plates not be hinged, if they are to copy the skull?
(d) Evaluate the club's statement that our joints move our bones.
questions.a: (a) The neck as a pivot and the elbow as a hinge. (b) The human shoulder is a ball and socket joint that allows forward, backward, sideways and circular movement; a hinge would let the arm move in one direction only, so it could not swing sideways or in a circle. (c) Skull bones are joined by fixed joints that cannot move, which keeps the brain safe even when the body moves; folding plates would not protect it. (d) The statement is wrong: joints allow movement but cannot move bones on their own; muscles contract and pull on bones through tendons.
s: (a) Neck = pivot and elbow = hinge are correct
(b) A hinge allows one direction only; no sideways or circular arm movement
(c) Skull bones are fixed, keeping the brain safe
(d) Wrong: muscles pulling through tendons move bones; joints only allow movement

questions.a: (a) It is a series of small bones called vertebrae; it supports the body and helps us stand upright. (b) The cartilage disc between each vertebra cushions and allows flexibility. (c) The ribs are attached to the spine at the back and to the breastbone (sternum) at the front, and are joined by flexible cartilage. (d) The flexible rib cage expands, increasing the space in the chest, so air moves into the lungs. (e) Breathing depends on the rib cage moving; an injury to the ribs makes this expansion painful and difficult.
s: (a) Made of vertebrae; supports the body and keeps it upright
(b) Cartilage discs between vertebrae
(c) Attached to the spine and sternum, joined by flexible cartilage
(d) Rib cage expands, chest space increases, air moves into the lungs
(e) Injured ribs make the needed movement painful and difficult
